text:
The complaints tend to cluster around a few things:

- **Accounts or payments being frozen or reviewed.** Banks have to monitor for fraud and money laundering, but customers can be frustrated when legitimate money is held and they can’t get a clear explanation or timeline.
- **Hard-to-reach support.** Because Monzo is app-first and has no branches, people can feel stuck in chat—especially when an urgent payment, account restriction or card issue needs sorting out.
- **Fraud and scam decisions.** Some customers disagree with Monzo’s decision not to refund a scam or unauthorised payment. Ombudsman decisions show these disputes do reach independent review; one recent report found the Ombudsman disagreed with Monzo in about 34% of the fraud cases it decided in 2025. That figure applies to cases escalated to and decided by the Ombudsman, not to all Monzo customers or all claims.
- **Refunds and disputes taking a long time.** Card-payment disputes can depend on evidence and the merchant’s response, and customers may find the process slow or unclear.
- **App-only limitations and glitches.** Login problems, outages or a feature not working can be more disruptive when the app is also the main way to access the account and contact support.

There’s an important caveat: complaint sites and review pages over-represent people having a bad experience. Monzo’s own published complaints data for the six months to 31 March 2026 lists “product performance / features” as the main cause in its banking-and-credit-card category, and says about 24% of those complaints were upheld. That’s useful context, but it doesn’t tell you how likely an individual customer is to have a problem.

In short: people often like Monzo when everything works, but the digital-first model can feel unforgiving when money is held, a dispute drags on, or the app is the thing that’s gone wrong.
